summary.text: Telescoping two related binomial sums gives a two-dimensional recurrence with a quadratic transfer matrix; multiplying consecutive transfers and eliminating the auxiliary component produces the scalar recurrence, with $P$ obtained from the upper-right entry $R_m$ after the affine change $x\mapsto m(x-1)$ and $Q$ by writing the even polynomial $R_{2m}(mx-m)$ as $Q(x^2)$. The reflection identity for the transfer matrix gives the required symmetry, while positivity of its blocks forces $R_m$ to alternate signs at the half-integers $-j/2$; the resulting $2m$ distinct intermediate-value roots, together with the degree bound, exhaust all complex roots and the affine changes place them in the claimed intervals.

full_proof.text:
Fix an integer \(m\geq 1\). We construct the required polynomials from a two-dimensional recurrence for the sequence.

First, the coefficient definition of the sequence agrees with the binomial sum that we shall use. Indeed, for \(n>0\), expansion of
\[
 (1+x)^n(1-x)^{-n}
\]
gives
\[
 [x^{2n}]\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)^n
 =\sum_{j=0}^n \binom nj\binom{3n-j-1}{2n-j}.
\]
Putting \(k=n-j\), and taking complements in the second binomial coefficient, this becomes
\[
 a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}.
\]
We set \(a(0)=1\), as in the statement.

## 1. A two-dimensional recurrence for the binomial sum

For nonnegative integers \(n,k\), define
\[
 F(n,k)=\binom nk\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1},
 \qquad
 G(n,k)=\binom{n-1}{k}\binom{2n+k}{n-1},
\]
with the usual convention that a binomial coefficient is zero when its lower index exceeds its upper index. Define real sequences
\[
 A_0=1,
 \qquad
 A_n=\sum_{k=0}^nF(n,k)\quad(n\geq1),
\]
and
\[
 C_0=-1,
 \qquad
 C_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}G(n,k)\quad(n\geq1).
\]
Thus \(A_n=a(n)\).

We derive simultaneous recurrences for \(A_n,C_n\). The necessary summand identities can be checked directly from factorials. For \(n\geq1\) and indices in the indicated ranges, one has
\[
 (k+1)(n+k+1)F(n,k+1)=(n-k)(2n+k)F(n,k),                 \tag{1}
\]
\[
 F(n,k)=\frac{n(n+1-k)(n+k+1)}{(n+1)(2n+k)(2n+k+1)}F(n+1,k),              \tag{2}
\]
\[
 nG(n,k)=(k+1)F(n,k+1),                                  \tag{3}
\]
and consequently
\[
 G(n,k)=\frac{(n-k)(2n+k)}{n(n+k+1)}F(n,k),               \tag{4}
\]
\[
 G(n,k)=\frac{(n+1-k)(n-k)}{(n+1)(2n+k+1)}F(n+1,k).       \tag{5}
\]
At an endpoint where a displayed quotient is not needed, the same identity follows from the vanishing of the relevant binomial coefficient. For example, (1) at \(k=n\) says that both sides are zero. All other cases follow by inserting
\(\binom rs=r!/(s!(r-s)!)\) and cancelling adjacent factorials.

For the telescoping calculation, introduce the rational functions
\[
 U(n,k)=
 \frac{k(k+n+1)\bigl(10kn^2+10kn+2k-28n^3-47n^2-25n-4\bigr)}
 {(k+2n)(n+1)(k+2n+1)},
\]
\[
 V(n,k)=
 \frac{k(2n+1)(k-n-1)\bigl(4kn+2k+3n^2+7n+2\bigr)}
 {(k+2n)(n+1)(k+2n+1)}.
\]
For \(n\geq1\) and \(0\leq k\leq n+1\), substitution of (1), (2), and (5), followed by clearing the nonzero denominators, gives the two polynomial identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(2n+1)(2n+2)F(n+1,k)
 -(32n^2+34n+8)F(n,k)\\
 &\hspace{35mm}-(20n^2+20n+4)G(n,k)\\
 &=U(n,k+1)F(n+1,k+1)-U(n,k)F(n+1,k),                    \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(2n+1)(2n+2)G(n+1,k)
 -(20n^2+18n+4)F(n,k)\\
 &\hspace{35mm}-(12n^2+10n+2)G(n,k)\\
 &=V(n,k+1)F(n+1,k+1)-V(n,k)F(n+1,k).                    \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
These are ordinary rational-function identities: after replacing each summand by the ratios above, both sides have the same common factor \(F(n+1,k)\), and clearing
\((k+2n)(n+1)(k+2n+1)(k+1)(n+k+2)\) reduces each assertion to expansion of the displayed polynomials.

Sum (6) and (7) over \(k=0,1,\ldots,n+1\). The right sides telescope. Their lower endpoint terms vanish because \(U(n,0)=V(n,0)=0\), while their upper endpoint terms contain \(F(n+1,n+2)=0\). Also
\(F(n,n+1)=0\), \(G(n,n)=G(n,n+1)=0\), and
\(G(n+1,n+1)=0\). Therefore, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
 (2n+1)(2n+2)A_{n+1}
 =(32n^2+34n+8)A_n+(20n^2+20n+4)C_n,                    \tag{8}
\]
\[
 (2n+1)(2n+2)C_{n+1}
 =(20n^2+18n+4)A_n+(12n^2+10n+2)C_n.                    \tag{9}
\]
The case \(n=0\) is checked directly: \(A_0=1,C_0=-1,A_1=2,C_1=1\), and these values satisfy both (8) and (9). Thus (8) and (9) hold for every \(n\geq0\).

Now put
\[
 v_n=\binom{A_n}{2A_n+4C_n}
\]
and define the polynomial matrix
\[
 T(x)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 22x^2+24x+6&5x^2+5x+1\\
 100x^2+100x+24&22x^2+20x+4
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Taking the first row of the equation below gives (8), and taking the second row gives twice (8) plus four times (9). Hence
\[
 T(n)v_n=(2n+1)(2n+2)v_{n+1}                              \tag{10}
\]
for all \(n\geq0\).

## 2. Products of transition matrices

For a nonnegative integer \(r\), define
\[
 B_0(x)=I,
 \qquad
 B_{r+1}(x)=T(x+r)B_r(x).
\]
Thus
\[
 B_r(x)=T(x+r-1)\cdots T(x+1)T(x).
\]
Splitting such a product into two consecutive blocks gives
\[
 B_{r+s}(x)=B_s(x+r)B_r(x).                               \tag{11}
\]
Let
\[
 R_r(x)=(B_r(x))_{01},                                    \tag{12}
\]
the upper-right entry. Because every entry of every \(T(x+j)\) has degree at most two, every entry of \(B_r(x)\), and in particular \(R_r(x)\), has degree at most \(2r\).

Define also
\[
 S_r(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{2r-1}(2x+j+1).
\]
Repeated use of (10) gives
\[
 B_r(n)v_n=S_r(n)v_{n+r}                                  \tag{13}
\]
for all nonnegative integers \(n,r\). Indeed, the assertion is immediate for \(r=0\), and the induction step uses
\[
 S_{r+1}(x)=\bigl(2(x+r)+1\bigr)\bigl(2(x+r)+2\bigr)S_r(x).
\]

A direct determinant calculation gives
\[
 \det T(x)=-(2x+1)^2(2x)(2x+2).                           \tag{14}
\]
Using multiplicativity of determinants, or induction together with the preceding recurrence for \(S_r\), it follows that
\[
 \det B_r(x)=(-1)^rS_r(x)S_r\left(x-\frac12\right).       \tag{15}
\]

We next eliminate the second coordinate from two adjacent block equations. We use the following elementary \(2\times2\) identity. Suppose
\[
 Mu=sv,\qquad Nv=tw,
\]
where \(s\neq0\), and suppose \(\det M=sd\). Then
\[
 tM_{01}w_0+dN_{01}u_0=(NM)_{01}v_0.                     \tag{16}
\]
To see this, write the two coordinate equations of \(Mu=sv\) and the first coordinate equation of \(Nv=tw\). Substitute these into the difference between the two sides of (16); after multiplication by \(s\), the remaining coefficient of \(N_{01}u_0\) is precisely
\(M_{00}M_{11}-M_{01}M_{10}-\det M=0\). Since \(s\neq0\), (16) follows.

Apply (16) with
\[
 M=B_m(l),\quad N=B_m(l+m),\quad
 u=v_l,\quad v=v_{l+m},\quad w=v_{l+2m},
\]
\[
 s=S_m(l),\quad t=S_m(l+m),\quad
 d=(-1)^mS_m\left(l-\frac12\right).
\]
Here \(l\geq0\), so every factor of \(S_m(l)\) is positive; in particular \(s\neq0\). Equations (13) give the two required matrix-vector equations, and (15) gives \(\det M=sd\). Finally, by (11),
\(NM=B_{2m}(l)\). Since the first coordinate of \(v_j\) is \(A_j\), identity (16) becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
&S_m(l+m)R_m(l)A_{l+2m}
 +(-1)^mS_m\left(l-\frac12\right)R_m(l+m)A_l\\
&\hspace{42mm}=R_{2m}(l)A_{l+m}.                          \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the recurrence from which the desired one will be obtained.

## 3. Reflection and zeros of \(R_r\)

For a matrix
\(M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), define
\[
 \Phi(M)=\begin{pmatrix}d&b\\c&a\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A direct multiplication shows
\[
 \Phi(MN)=\Phi(N)\Phi(M).                                 \tag{18}
\]
Direct substitution in the four entries of \(T\) also gives
\[
 T(-x-1)=\Phi(T(x)).                                      \tag{19}
\]
Using (18), (19), and induction on the length of a block, we obtain
\[
 B_r(-x-r)=\Phi(B_r(x)).                                  \tag{20}
\]
The operation \(\Phi\) leaves the upper-right entry unchanged, so
\[
 R_r(-x-r)=R_r(x).                                        \tag{21}
\]

We now locate all zeros of \(R_r\) for \(r\geq1\). Call a real \(2\times2\) matrix good if all its entries are nonnegative and both diagonal entries are positive, and strict if all its entries are positive. Products of good matrices are good. A strict matrix times a good matrix is strict, as is a good matrix times a strict matrix. Also \(\Phi\) preserves both properties.

For \(x\geq0\), every entry of \(T(x)\) is positive. Consequently \(B_s(x)\) is good for every \(s\geq0\), and is strict when \(s\geq1\). On the other hand, direct evaluation gives
\[
 T\left(-\frac12\right)
 =\begin{pmatrix}-\frac12&-\frac14\\-1&-\frac12\end{pmatrix},            \tag{22}
\]
so \(-T(-1/2)\) is strict.

For \(0\leq q\leq r\), splitting the product at the point where its argument crosses zero and using (20) yields
\[
 B_r(-q)=B_{r-q}(0)\,\Phi(B_q(0)).                        \tag{23}
\]
The upper-right entry of this product is strictly positive. If \(q=0\), this follows from the strictness of \(B_r(0)\); if \(q>0\), the second factor is strict, and the first is good (including when it is the identity). Therefore
\[
 R_r(-q)>0\qquad(0\leq q\leq r).                         \tag{24}
\]

Similarly, for \(0\leq q<r\), splitting at the unique factor with argument \(-1/2\) gives
\[
 B_r\left(-q-\frac12\right)
 =B_{r-q-1}\left(\frac12\right)
  T\left(-\frac12\right)
  \Phi\left(B_q\left(\frac12\right)\right).              \tag{25}
\]
The first and third factors are good, and replacing the middle factor by its negative makes the resulting product strict. Hence its upper-right entry is positive, and therefore
\[
 R_r\left(-q-\frac12\right)<0\qquad(0\leq q<r).           \tag{26}
\]
Combining (24) and (26), for every integer \(j\) with \(0\leq j\leq2r\),
\[
 (-1)^jR_r\left(-\frac j2\right)>0.                       \tag{27}
\]
Thus the values at each pair of consecutive points
\(-j/2\) and \(-(j+1)/2\) have opposite signs. By continuity, for each
\(j=0,1,\ldots,2r-1\), \(R_r\) has a zero in the open interval
\[
 \left(-\frac{j+1}{2},-\frac j2\right).                  \tag{28}
\]
These \(2r\) intervals are disjoint, so the zeros are distinct. Since we already know that \(\deg R_r\leq2r\), it follows that
\[
 \deg R_r=2r,                                             \tag{29}
\]
and these are all its complex zeros. In particular, every complex zero of \(R_r\) is real and belongs to \([-r,0]\). Notice that (27) also shows directly that \(R_r\) is not the zero polynomial.

## 4. Construction and root properties of \(P\) and \(Q\)

Define
\[
 P(x)=R_m(mx-m),                                          \tag{30}
\]
and first define the auxiliary polynomial
\[
 H(x)=R_{2m}(mx-m).                                       \tag{31}
\]
Because \(m\neq0\), composition with the nonconstant affine polynomial \(mx-m\) does not alter degree. Hence, by (29),
\[
 \deg P=2m,\qquad \deg H=4m.                              \tag{32}
\]

The reflection identity (21) gives the symmetry of \(P\). Indeed,
\[
 P(1-x)=R_m(-mx)=R_m(mx-m)=P(x),                          \tag{33}
\]
where the second equality is (21) applied with argument \(mx-m\).

If \(z\in\mathbb C\) is a zero of \(P\), then \(mz-m\) is a zero of \(R_m\). By the root location just proved, \(mz-m\) is real and its real part lies in \([-m,0]\). Since \(m>0\), this says
\[
 \operatorname{Im}z=0,
 \qquad 0\leq \operatorname{Re}z\leq1.                  \tag{34}
\]
Thus all zeros of \(P\) are real and in \([0,1]\).

The same reflection identity shows that \(H\) is even:
\[
 H(-x)=R_{2m}(-mx-m)=R_{2m}(mx-m)=H(x).                   \tag{35}
\]
A real polynomial is even exactly when all its odd-degree coefficients vanish. Therefore there is a unique real polynomial \(Q\) such that
\[
 H(x)=Q(x^2).                                             \tag{36}
\]
Explicitly, if \(H(x)=\sum_jh_jx^j\), then
\(Q(y)=\sum_kh_{2k}y^k\). Since \(\deg H=4m\), equation (36) gives
\[
 \deg Q=2m.                                               \tag{37}
\]

Suppose now that \(z\in\mathbb C\) satisfies \(Q(z^2)=0\). By (36), \(H(z)=0\), so \(mz-m\) is a zero of \(R_{2m}\). Every such zero is real and lies in \([-2m,0]\). As \(m>0\), it follows that
\[
 \operatorname{Im}z=0,
 \qquad -1\leq\operatorname{Re}z\leq1.                  \tag{38}
\]
This is exactly the required root assertion for \(Q(x^2)\).

## 5. Conversion of the block recurrence to the stated recurrence

Let \(n\geq1\) and put
\[
 l=m(n-1)=mn-m.
\]
Then
\[
 l+m=mn,
 \qquad l+2m=m(n+1).
\]
Thus the three sequence terms in (17) are respectively
\[
 A_{l+2m}=a(m(n+1))=b(n+1),
\quad A_{l+m}=a(mn)=b(n),
\quad A_l=a(m(n-1))=b(n-1).
\]
By (30),
\[
 R_m(l)=R_m(mn-m)=P(n).                                  \tag{39}
\]
Also, using reflection (21),
\[
 P(-n)=R_m(-mn-m)=R_m(mn)=R_m(l+m).                      \tag{40}
\]
By (31) and (36),
\[
 R_{2m}(l)=R_{2m}(mn-m)=H(n)=Q(n^2).                     \tag{41}
\]

It remains only to identify the two products in (17). Directly from the definition of \(S_m\),
\[
 S_m(l+m)=S_m(mn)
 =\prod_{j=0}^{2m-1}(2mn+j+1)
 =\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k).                               \tag{42}
\]
For the other product,
\[
 S_m\left(l-\frac12\right)
 =\prod_{j=0}^{2m-1}(2mn-2m+j).
\]
Reversing the order by putting \(k=2m-j\) gives
\[
 S_m\left(l-\frac12\right)
 =\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn-k).                               \tag{43}
\]

Substituting (39)--(43) into (17) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k)\right)P(n)b(n+1)\\
&\quad+(-1)^m\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn-k)\right)P(-n)b(n-1)
 =Q(n^2)b(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every integer \(n\geq1\). Equations (32), (33), (34), (37), and (38) give respectively the required degrees, symmetry, and root-location properties. Hence the polynomials \(P\) and \(Q\) constructed in (30) and (36) satisfy every assertion of the conjecture.
